screens.title: STL Containers: Purpose and Practical Choices
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll get a clear, practical view of the containers in the C++ Standard Template Library. Containers are pre-built, generic data structures that store collections of objects and manage memory for you. They let you focus on your program’s logic rather than reinventing arrays, lists, and hash tables. You’ll learn how vectors act like dynamic arrays, how lists implement doubly linked sequences, and how associative containers such as map and unordered_map store key-value pairs with predictable performance trade-offs. I’ll show concrete examples you can use immediately, and I’ll also point out common pitfalls — like using a vector for many middle insertions or expecting a list to give fast random access. By the end of this chapter you should be able to match a problem to the right container and understand the cost of operations you perform. Think about a real problem you might write: do you need sorted keys, constant-time lookup, or fast insertions in the middle? That question is the core of choosing correctly.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › STL Containers Overview
STL Containers: Purpose and Practical Choices
Understand why STL containers exist, compare common types, and learn to pick the right one for everyday C++ tasks.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson
How containers manage elements, container categories, and practical selection rules. Examples for vector, list, map, unordered_map, and set will ground the ideas.
Why it matters

Picking the wrong container leads to performance problems and memory surprises. Using STL saves development time and gives you consistent, tested behaviors for common patterns like dynamic arrays and associative lookups.

Explore Key Topics
Vector
Dynamic array, O(1) index access, amortized push_back.
List
Doubly linked nodes, O(1) insert/erase with iterator, no random access.
Maps & Sets
Associative containers for keys, choose sorted vs hashed based on ordering needs.
Concept map
Containers
Sequence
vector, list — ordered collections
Associative
map, unordered_map, set — key-based access
Set
Unique key storage, membership testing
Performance
Time complexity guides container choice
Starting point
If you need a simple growable array and index access, start with std::vector. Consider other containers only when specific insertion, ordering, or lookup requirements demand them.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you will build a practical understanding of STL containers and when to use them. First, you’ll learn the purpose and structure of the STL and why templates make reusable container code possible. Next, you’ll identify and differentiate common containers — vector, list, map, unordered_map, and set — and understand their A P I surface and typical operations. You will practice using std::vector for dynamic arrays, including push_back, insert, erase, and safe access via at(). You’ll learn when std::list is the better choice because of constant-time insertions and deletions when you already have an iterator to the right position. Finally, you’ll master associative containers: map for ordered key-value storage and unordered_map for hashed lookups. Each objective pairs a concrete coding skill with a reason it matters, so you leave with usable patterns, not just names.

screens.title: What is a Container in the STL?
screens.narratorSegment: A container is an object that stores a collection of other objects and manages the memory needed to hold them. In the STL, containers are template classes so the same container code works with many element types without duplication. That templated design is why containers integrate cleanly with algorithms and iterators — they expose uniform member functions and iterator types so algorithms can operate on many containers. Concretely, containers provide operations for insertion, removal, traversal, and often element access. The important idea is responsibility: containers manage storage and provide access semantics; your code uses those semantics rather than reimplementing memory management. A common misconception is to treat containers as interchangeable; they are not. Each container has different performance guarantees and access capabilities. For example, vector offers random access by index with O(1) time, while a list offers O(1) insertion when you already hold the iterator but no O(1) random access. Remember: choose a container for how you will access and modify elements, not only for its name. As a quick example, if you need predictable sorted iteration by key, an associative container like map is appropriate because it maintains ordering. What operations will your program perform most often?

keyIdea.title: Container responsibility
keyIdea.text: Containers store and manage elements; templates let the same container code work with different element types and pair well with algorithms and iterators.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is a Container?
An STL container is a templated object that stores elements and provides operations for insertion, removal, and traversal while managing memory.
Definition
A templated class that stores multiple elements and exposes iterators and member functions to manipulate them.
Why templates?
Templates let containers work with any element type while keeping a single, tested implementation.
Common misconception
Containers are not interchangeable — each offers different access patterns and performance guarantees.
Key Takeaway

Pick containers based on required access patterns, insertion patterns, and ordering guarantees, not by name alone.

Analogy: Containers are toolboxes
Like a toolbox organized for different tasks, each container groups operations and guarantees. You choose the toolbox before starting the job.
Concrete example
If you need sorted traversal of key-value pairs, use std::map so iteration yields keys in order without extra sorting steps.
Check your understanding
  • What operations does your program perform most often: random access, frequent mid-list inserts, or key lookups?
  • If you need ordering by key, is unordered_map acceptable? (No — unordered_map is not ordered.)
  • Would a custom container be better than STL for your case? Usually not unless you have specialized constraints.

screens.title: std::vector: Dynamic Array Basics
screens.narratorSegment: std::vector is a dynamic array: it stores elements contiguously and grows or shrinks as needed. This gives you O(1) random access by index, so retrieving the element at a known index is fast and cache-friendly. Common operations include push_back to append, pop_back to remove the last element, insert and erase for arbitrary positions, and size and capacity queries to inspect current usage and allocated space. A practical example is keeping a list of product names when you mostly add to the end: push_back is ideal here. Use at() for bounds-checked access during development to avoid undefined behavior from out-of-range index use. A common gotcha is assuming push_back is always O(1): it is amortized O(1) because occasional reallocation and element copying occur when capacity runs out. To control that cost, call reserve when you know an approximate final size. Consider using erase carefully because removing from mid-vector requires shifting elements and costs O(N). In short, use vector when you need fast index access and growth at the end, and reserve or careful insertion patterns to manage performance. std::vector: Dynamic Array Basics means use std::vector for contiguous storage and fast index access; manage capacity with reserve to reduce reallocation cost.. In practical terms, typical operations, safe access, and a concrete example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Vector summary
keyIdea.text: Use std::vector for contiguous storage and fast index access; manage capacity with reserve to reduce reallocation cost.

content.html:
Definition
std::vector basics
Contiguous dynamic array with indexed access and dynamic resizing.
Key operations
  • push_back, pop_back — append and remove last
  • insert, erase — insert or remove at arbitrary positions (O(N) shifts)
  • size, capacity, reserve — manage growth and allocation
Common pitfall
Using [] out of bounds causes undefined behavior. Prefer at() when you need safety checks during development.
Key Takeaway

std::vector is the go-to sequence when you want fast index access and growth at the end; manage capacity to avoid occasional costly reallocations.

Code example
<#include <iostream>>
<#include <vector>>

int main() {
  std::vector<int> numbers; // empty vector
  numbers.push_back(10);
  numbers.push_back(20);
  numbers.push_back(30);

  // Access
  std::cout << "First element: " << numbers[0] << std::endl;
  std::cout << "Second element: " << numbers.at(1) << std::endl;

  // Size and capacity
  std::cout << "Size: " << numbers.size() << std::endl;
  std::cout << "Capacity: " << numbers.capacity() << std::endl;

  // Insert and erase
  numbers.insert(numbers.begin() + 1, 15);
  numbers.erase(numbers.begin() + 2);

  return 0;
}
Concrete example
Use vector to store sensor readings that you mostly append to and occasionally index by position for analysis.

screens.title: Vector Performance: Size, Capacity, and Amortized Costs
screens.narratorSegment: Vectors grow by allocating a larger contiguous block and moving elements when capacity is exhausted. This makes push_back amortized O(1): most append operations are constant time, but occasionally the vector reallocates and copies all elements, which costs O(N) for that operation. To limit those expensive reallocations, call reserve with an anticipated size to pre-allocate capacity. Doing so keeps push_back operations reliably fast and reduces memory churn. Another performance point is insert and erase in the middle of a vector: because storage is contiguous, inserting requires shifting all subsequent elements, which is O(N). If your program frequently inserts in the middle, a vector may be a poor choice despite its fast indexing. A useful rule is to ask how often you insert at non-end positions and whether random access is critical. For occasional middle insertions and heavy indexing, vector still often wins due to cache locality; for very frequent mid-list structural changes, consider list. Finally, measure: premature optimization is a trap, but when performance matters, inspect size, capacity, and measure reallocation counts. Vector Performance: Size, Capacity, and Amortized Costs means use reserve to reduce reallocations; avoid frequent middle insertions on vectors because they require shifting elements and cost o(n).. In practical terms, understand reallocation, reserve, and the cost of mid-vector modifications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
Vector reallocation lifecycle
How vector grows and what it costs you.
Performance focus
Normal append
push_back uses available capacity. Operation is constant time.
Reallocation event
When capacity is full, vector allocates a larger block and copies elements — an O(N) operation.
Avoid frequent reallocations
Call reserve(expected_size) to pre-allocate buffer and keep push_back fast and predictable.
Mid-vector modifications
Insertions or deletions away from the end require shifting subsequent elements, which costs O(N). If your workload performs these often, consider an alternative container like std::list or redesign to batch modifications.
Concrete example
Appending 10k sensor readings benefits from reserve to avoid multiple reallocations; inserting a reading at position 0 each time is expensive due to shifting.
Misconception check
Vector is not always fastest: its cache friendliness helps, but many mid-list operations can undo that advantage.

screens.title: std::list: Doubly Linked List Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: std::list implements a doubly linked list where each element is stored in a node that contains pointers to the previous and next nodes. Because nodes are allocated separately, elements are not contiguous in memory. The main advantage is that insertion and deletion at any position are O(1) once you have an iterator to that position, since only neighboring pointers are updated. This makes list a good choice when your program frequently inserts or removes elements in the middle of a sequence and you already have iterators or positions available. But list has several trade-offs: there is no operator[] for random access, so obtaining the nth element requires traversal O(N). Lists also consume more memory per element because of pointer overhead, and pointer chasing reduces cache locality which can make traversal slower than a vector for sequential access. A common mistake is choosing list for occasional insertions: often vector plus occasional shifts remains faster due to cache and overall lower memory overhead. Use list when many structural modifications dominate and random access is not required. std::list: Doubly Linked List Behavior means std::list gives o(1) local insert/delete with iterator but lacks random access and uses extra memory; choose it when mid-sequence structural changes dominate.. In practical terms, how nodes, iterators, and constant-time local changes work. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: List summary
keyIdea.text: std::list gives O(1) local insert/delete with iterator but lacks random access and uses extra memory; choose it when mid-sequence structural changes dominate.

content.html:
Definition
std::list behavior
A doubly linked collection of nodes allowing constant-time insertion and deletion given an iterator.
Benefits
O(1) insertion and deletion at arbitrary positions when you already have an iterator.
Trade-offs
  • No random access; operator[] is not available.
  • Extra memory per element for node pointers.
  • Poor cache locality can slow linear traversals compared to vector.
Key Takeaway

Choose std::list when you have many mid-sequence inserts/removals and iterators are available; avoid it solely for semantical simplicity.

Code example
<#include <list>>
<#include <iostream>>

int main() {
  std::list<std::string> names;
  names.push_back("Alice");
  names.push_front("Charlie");
  names.push_back("Bob");

  auto it = names.begin();
  std::advance(it, 1); // move to second element
  names.insert(it, "David");

  names.erase(names.begin()); // remove first element
  return 0;
}
Concrete scenario
Use list for an editor buffer where you insert and remove characters or lines often and you hold iterators to edit points.

screens.title: Associative Containers: map vs unordered_map
screens.narratorSegment: Associative containers store key-value pairs and allow lookups by key. std::map stores elements in sorted order by key, typically using a self-balancing binary search tree under the hood, which gives O(log N) insertion, lookup, and deletion with predictable worst-case bounds. This sorted ordering is useful for range queries and predictable iteration. In contrast, std::unordered_map uses a hash table to store elements and offers average O(1) insertion, lookup, and deletion, with the possibility of worst-case O(N) in the presence of many collisions. Use unordered_map when you need fast average lookups and don't care about order. Use map when you need sorted keys or guaranteed logarithmic costs. A common misconception is that unordered_map is always faster; while average operations are constant time, iteration order is unspecified and can vary. If predictable key order matters, choose map. Another practical note: custom key types in unordered_map require a hash function; built-in types already have std::hash specializations. Think about whether you will iterate in key order or need the fastest per-element lookup when deciding between these two. Associative Containers: map vs unordered_map means pick std::map for sorted keys and guaranteed o(log n) behavior; pick std::unordered_map for average o(1) lookups when order doesn't matter.. In practical terms, sorted tree vs hash table — guarantees, average costs, and iteration order. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Associative choice
keyIdea.text: Pick std::map for sorted keys and guaranteed O(log N) behavior; pick std::unordered_map for average O(1) lookups when order doesn't matter.

content.html:
Comparison
std::map (sorted)
Typically implemented as a balanced tree, supports ordered iteration and O(log N) operations.
When to use
When you need keys in sorted order or range queries, or when worst-case logarithmic performance is required.
<#include <map>>
std::map<std::string, int> ages;
ages["Alice"] = 30;
ages["Bob"] = 25;
// Iteration yields sorted keys
for (const auto &p : ages) {
  // p.first is key, p.second is value
}
Comparison
std::unordered_map (hashed)
Implements a hash table for average O(1) lookup, insertion, and deletion; iteration order is unspecified.
When to use
When you prioritize average lookup speed and do not require sorted keys.
<#include <unordered_map>>
std::unordered_map<std::string, int> scores;
scores["Math"] = 95;
// Fast lookup by key on average
int m = scores["Math"];

screens.title: Sets: Unique-Value Containers
screens.narratorSegment: Sets store unique keys without associated values. std::set keeps elements in sorted order and offers O(log N) insert, lookup, and delete — similar to map but without values. std::unordered_set uses a hash table to provide average O(1) operations, sacrificing ordering for speed. The primary use-case for sets is efficient membership testing and ensuring uniqueness, for example tracking discontinued product names so you can quickly check if a product is discontinued. A tricky point is that sets only store keys, so if you need to associate additional data, prefer a map or unordered_map. Another important consideration is iteration: if you need to process keys in sorted order for reporting, use std::set; if you only need fast membership checks with no ordering requirements, choose std::unordered_set. A frequent misconception is that a set is always better for membership; vector with linear search may be simpler for tiny collections, but for large collections a set or unordered_set provides clear performance advantages. When you need unique items and predictable ordered iteration, for example producing an alphabetized report.

Inventory: containers combined

  1. Add product name to vector with push_back.
  2. Set or update stock in std::map using stock[name] = qty.

// add product
void addProduct(std::vector<std::string>& products, const std::string &name) {

// remove using remove-erase

screens.title: Choosing the Right Container: Decision Guide
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right container is a question of access patterns, modification patterns, and ordering requirements. Ask four questions: do you need random access by index? Do you append frequently to the end? Do you perform many insert/delete operations in the middle? Do you require ordered iteration by key or only fast lookups? If you need random access and mostly append, std::vector is typically the best. If you perform many mid-list insertions and hold iterators, consider std::list. For key-value storage where you need sorted keys and range queries, std::map is appropriate; if you need the fastest average lookup and order doesn't matter, std::unordered_map is the better fit. For unique-key membership, pick std::set for sorted membership or std::unordered_set for hashed performance. A common mistake is optimizing for a single operation without considering the rest of the workload; measure and prefer simpler containers until profiling shows a bottleneck. Keep in mind memory overhead and cache effects: contiguous storage tends to perform better for sequential access. Use this checklist while designing and revisit choices after profiling. screens.title: Complexity Recap: Big-O for Common Containers
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the time complexity of common operations is essential to picking containers. Here's a concise summary you should internalize: for std::vector, index access is O(1), push_back is amortized O(1), but insert and erase in the middle are O(N). For std::list, insertion and deletion at a known position are O(1) but random access is O(N). For std::map, lookups, insertions, and deletions are O(log N) due to its tree structure. For std::unordered_map, these operations are average O(1) but can degrade to O(N) in pathological hash-collision cases. For std::set and std::unordered_set, think similarly to map and unordered_map respectively, but without values. A useful learner exercise is to imagine scaling from 10 to 10 million elements and reason how each container's complexity affects runtime. Complexity doesn't tell the whole story: constants, memory layout, and cache locality also influence real performance. Use these Big-O rules as a guide and confirm with profiling on your real data. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Every developer hits the same set of container mistakes. First, out-of-bounds access in vector using operator[] can cause undefined behavior and subtle bugs — prefer at() for safety during testing. Second, choosing std::list because you think insertions will be cheaper without analyzing position-finding costs is common; lists only save work when you already have the iterator to the insertion point. Third, using unordered_map when your code needs sorted iteration can lead to surprises because unordered_map iteration order is unspecified. Fourth, failing to reserve capacity for large known sizes causes many reallocations and performance jitter. Best practices: prefer vector as a default for sequences, measure hot paths, use reserve when sizes are known, and select associative containers based on ordering and lookup requirements. When combining containers, document why each was chosen so future maintainers understand the trade-offs. Finally, test with realistic data sizes: small data behave differently than large-scale workloads due to cache and allocation patterns. Which of your recent programs could benefit from one of these changes? Common Mistakes and Best Practices means default to vector for sequences, use reserve when possible, pick lists only when iterators are available for mid-list work, and match associative containers to ordering needs.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Safety, realistic data, and measured choices matter more than theoretical purity.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll get a clear, practical view of the containers in the C++ Standard Template Library. Containers are pre-built, generic data structures that store collections of objects and manage memory for you. They let you focus on your program’s logic rather than reinventing arrays, lists, and hash tables. You’ll learn how vectors act like dynamic arrays, how lists implement doubly linked sequences, and how associative containers such as map and unordered_map store key-value pairs with predictable performance trade-offs. I’ll show concrete examples you can use immediately, and I’ll also point out common pitfalls — like using a vector for many middle insertions or expecting a list to give fast random access. By the end of this chapter you should be able to match a problem to the right container and understand the cost of operations you perform. Think about a real problem you might write: do you need sorted keys, constant-time lookup, or fast insertions in the middle? That question is the core of choosing correctly.

Over the next screens you will build a practical understanding of STL containers and when to use them. First, you’ll learn the purpose and structure of the STL and why templates make reusable container code possible. Next, you’ll identify and differentiate common containers — vector, list, map, unordered_map, and set — and understand their A P I surface and typical operations. You will practice using std::vector for dynamic arrays, including push_back, insert, erase, and safe access via at(). You’ll learn when std::list is the better choice because of constant-time insertions and deletions when you already have an iterator to the right position. Finally, you’ll master associative containers: map for ordered key-value storage and unordered_map for hashed lookups. Each objective pairs a concrete coding skill with a reason it matters, so you leave with usable patterns, not just names.

This second objectives slide focuses on doing. You will implement small, specific functions that use STL containers: manage a list of product names with std::vector, maintain product stock with std::map, and track discontinued items with std::unordered_set. These tasks exercise adding, removing, updating, and checking membership — the most used container operations. Working through the inventory example trains you to combine containers correctly: vectors for ordered lists, maps for sorted key-value stock, and unordered sets for quick membership checks. The activity also surfaces common pitfalls to avoid, such as using vector erase naive loops or assuming unordered_map preserves insertion order. By completing the activity you’ll see performance implications in practice and be able to defend your container choices in simple design decisions. Learning Objectives — Practice and Assessment means complete a small inventory system exercise that integrates vector, map, and unordered_set so you practice combining containers with appropriate operations.. In practical terms, concrete tasks and the hands-on activity you will complete. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A container is an object that stores a collection of other objects and manages the memory needed to hold them. In the STL, containers are template classes so the same container code works with many element types without duplication. That templated design is why containers integrate cleanly with algorithms and iterators — they expose uniform member functions and iterator types so algorithms can operate on many containers. Concretely, containers provide operations for insertion, removal, traversal, and often element access. The important idea is responsibility: containers manage storage and provide access semantics; your code uses those semantics rather than reimplementing memory management. A common misconception is to treat containers as interchangeable; they are not. Each container has different performance guarantees and access capabilities. For example, vector offers random access by index with O(1) time, while a list offers O(1) insertion when you already hold the iterator but no O(1) random access. Remember: choose a container for how you will access and modify elements, not only for its name. As a quick example, if you need predictable sorted iteration by key, an associative container like map is appropriate because it maintains ordering. What operations will your program perform most often?

std::vector is a dynamic array: it stores elements contiguously and grows or shrinks as needed. This gives you O(1) random access by index, so retrieving the element at a known index is fast and cache-friendly. Common operations include push_back to append, pop_back to remove the last element, insert and erase for arbitrary positions, and size and capacity queries to inspect current usage and allocated space. A practical example is keeping a list of product names when you mostly add to the end: push_back is ideal here. Use at() for bounds-checked access during development to avoid undefined behavior from out-of-range index use. A common gotcha is assuming push_back is always O(1): it is amortized O(1) because occasional reallocation and element copying occur when capacity runs out. To control that cost, call reserve when you know an approximate final size. Consider using erase carefully because removing from mid-vector requires shifting elements and costs O(N). In short, use vector when you need fast index access and growth at the end, and reserve or careful insertion patterns to manage performance. std::vector: Dynamic Array Basics means use std::vector for contiguous storage and fast index access; manage capacity with reserve to reduce reallocation cost.. In practical terms, typical operations, safe access, and a concrete example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Vectors grow by allocating a larger contiguous block and moving elements when capacity is exhausted. This makes push_back amortized O(1): most append operations are constant time, but occasionally the vector reallocates and copies all elements, which costs O(N) for that operation. To limit those expensive reallocations, call reserve with an anticipated size to pre-allocate capacity. Doing so keeps push_back operations reliably fast and reduces memory churn. Another performance point is insert and erase in the middle of a vector: because storage is contiguous, inserting requires shifting all subsequent elements, which is O(N). If your program frequently inserts in the middle, a vector may be a poor choice despite its fast indexing. A useful rule is to ask how often you insert at non-end positions and whether random access is critical. std::list implements a doubly linked list where each element is stored in a node that contains pointers to the previous and next nodes. Because nodes are allocated separately, elements are not contiguous in memory. The main advantage is that insertion and deletion at any position are O(1) once you have an iterator to that position, since only neighboring pointers are updated. This makes list a good choice when your program frequently inserts or removes elements in the middle of a sequence and you already have iterators or positions available. But list has several trade-offs: there is no operator[] for random access, so obtaining the nth element requires traversal O(N). Lists also consume more memory per element because of pointer overhead, and pointer chasing reduces cache locality which can make traversal slower than a vector for sequential access. A common mistake is choosing list for occasional insertions: often vector plus occasional shifts remains faster due to cache and overall lower memory overhead. Associative containers store key-value pairs and allow lookups by key. std::map stores elements in sorted order by key, typically using a self-balancing binary search tree under the hood, which gives O(log N) insertion, lookup, and deletion with predictable worst-case bounds. This sorted ordering is useful for range queries and predictable iteration. In contrast, std::unordered_map uses a hash table to store elements and offers average O(1) insertion, lookup, and deletion, with the possibility of worst-case O(N) in the presence of many collisions. Use unordered_map when you need fast average lookups and don't care about order. Use map when you need sorted keys or guaranteed logarithmic costs. A common misconception is that unordered_map is always faster; while average operations are constant time, iteration order is unspecified and can vary. If predictable key order matters, choose map. Another practical note: custom key types in unordered_map require a hash function; built-in types already have std::hash specializations. Think about whether you will iterate in key order or need the fastest per-element lookup when deciding between these two. Sets store unique keys without associated values. std::set keeps elements in sorted order and offers O(log N) insert, lookup, and delete — similar to map but without values. std::unordered_set uses a hash table to provide average O(1) operations, sacrificing ordering for speed. The primary use-case for sets is efficient membership testing and ensuring uniqueness, for example tracking discontinued product names so you can quickly check if a product is discontinued. A tricky point is that sets only store keys, so if you need to associate additional data, prefer a map or unordered_map. Another important consideration is iteration: if you need to process keys in sorted order for reporting, use std::set; if you only need fast membership checks with no ordering requirements, choose std::unordered_set. A frequent misconception is that a set is always better for membership; vector with linear search may be simpler for tiny collections, but for large collections a set or unordered_set provides clear performance advantages. Choosing the right container is a question of access patterns, modification patterns, and ordering requirements. Ask four questions: do you need random access by index? Do you append frequently to the end? Do you perform many insert/delete operations in the middle? Do you require ordered iteration by key or only fast lookups? If you need random access and mostly append, std::vector is typically the best. If you perform many mid-list insertions and hold iterators, consider std::list. For key-value storage where you need sorted keys and range queries, std::map is appropriate; if you need the fastest average lookup and order doesn't matter, std::unordered_map is the better fit. For unique-key membership, pick std::set for sorted membership or std::unordered_set for hashed performance. Understanding the time complexity of common operations is essential to picking containers. Here's a concise summary you should internalize: for std::vector, index access is O(1), push_back is amortized O(1), but insert and erase in the middle are O(N). For std::list, insertion and deletion at a known position are O(1) but random access is O(N). For std::map, lookups, insertions, and deletions are O(log N) due to its tree structure. For std::unordered_map, these operations are average O(1) but can degrade to O(N) in pathological hash-collision cases. For std::set and std::unordered_set, think similarly to map and unordered_map respectively, but without values. Every developer hits the same set of container mistakes. First, out-of-bounds access in vector using operator[] can cause undefined behavior and subtle bugs — prefer at() for safety during testing. Second, choosing std::list because you think insertions will be cheaper without analyzing position-finding costs is common; lists only save work when you already have the iterator to the insertion point. Third, using unordered_map when your code needs sorted iteration can lead to surprises because unordered_map iteration order is unspecified. Fourth, failing to reserve capacity for large known sizes causes many reallocations and performance jitter. Best practices: prefer vector as a default for sequences, measure hot paths, use reserve when sizes are known, and select associative containers based on ordering and lookup requirements. When combining containers, document why each was chosen so future maintainers understand the trade-offs. Finally, test with realistic data sizes: small data behave differently than large-scale workloads due to cache and allocation patterns. Keep these short concepts in mind as you apply containers: the STL provides templated containers that manage storage and expose iterators for algorithms. A container’s memory layout and iterator behavior determine performance: contiguous storage like vector is fast for indexing and sequential access, while node-based storage like list makes structural changes cheap when you already have an iterator. Associative containers organize data by key: map offers sorted keys with logarithmic guarantees, whereas unordered_map offers fast average lookup using hashing but without order guarantees. Finally, sets store unique keys and mirror map/unordered_map behavior for membership-only scenarios.
